script.opening: (Mother, tired, a bit defensive; Leo is at school.) "Leo's school have been on at me — they say he's got ADHD, he can't sit still, he's disruptive, doesn't listen, and they reckon he needs to be on medication for it. They more or less told me to come and get it sorted. So — can you prescribe something, or refer him for the tablets?"

facts.text: "He can't sit still, he's disruptive, he doesn't listen — that's what they keep saying. I couldn't tell you exactly when it started." Started in Year 3 (this year) with a new teacher. Has had two detentions. No school report brought, but can get one.

"Honestly, I'm not sure. He's a lively boy, but I've never really thought of it as a problem at home." Can concentrate for an hour on Lego or computer games. Gets distracted with homework. Was a "normal" toddler, met milestones.
"I don't really know what he thinks. They haven't said much about that side." He says the other kids laugh at him when he gets things wrong.

"Not that I know of, no one's checked his hearing. Sleep, I'd have to think about." If asked more: had lots of ear infections as a toddler; often says "what?"; snores loudly most nights and is hard to wake; goes to bed at 10.
"I'm not sure. I'd have to ask school." Struggles with reading. No SENCO involvement that she knows of.

If asked about home: "Nothing I want to go into. It's just me being worn out by it all." If asked gently and privately later: she and Leo's dad separated 8 months ago after a lot of arguing; Dad now sees him every other weekend. No violence to Leo. No social worker.
No medicines, no allergies, no heart problems, no fainting. Dad "was a nightmare at school" but never diagnosed with anything.

"I feel like they think it's my fault. School are always on at me. I thought if I came back with tablets they'd get off my back." "Part of me wonders if they're right. Part of me doesn't want him on strong tablets."

Tired and under pressure: "I just want something done." If the doctor dismisses it as naughtiness, become upset. If the doctor just prescribes or promises tablets, accept (the trap). If the doctor explains the process: "So what happens, then? Do we just wait?" and "How long does the referral take?" Pleased to learn she can ask for a school (SENCO) meeting.

ice.ideas: "School says it's ADHD — he needs the tablets."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — feeling blamed by school; worn out after a recent separation she doesn't want to discuss; torn about medication for her son.
ice.expectations: "A prescription, or a referral for the tablets."

cues: "They told me to come and get it sorted." — school pressure.
"Never really a problem at home." — not clearly across settings.
"Nothing I want to go into." — a home stressor to return to gently.

checkpoints.text: Neither dismisses nor rubber-stamps the school’s view — recognises ADHD as a SPECIALIST clinical diagnosis after structured multi-setting assessment, not diagnosed/medicated in primary care on a teacher’s report
Characterises the pattern (inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity), ONSET, PERVASIVENESS across settings (home and school) and degree of IMPAIRMENT — and gets the child’s perspective where possible

EXCLUDES/considers the differentials and contributors — hearing/vision, SLEEP disorder, learning difficulty, autism, anxiety/mood, attachment/TRAUMA/ACEs, SAFEGUARDING, family/social stress — as the key safety skill
Gathers MULTI-SOURCE information (school reports/observations, parent- and teacher-completed questionnaires, developmental/family history) to inform the referral rather than acting on a single report

Refers to the NEURODEVELOPMENTAL/ADHD pathway and manages expectations (timescales, specialist diagnosis, NICE NG87 staged treatment: information, support and environmental modifications first, then specialist-initiated medication at age 5+ if significant impairment persists after they are reviewed; no elimination diets) — supporting the family meanwhile (SENCO, strategies, support orgs)
Takes the school’s/mother’s concern seriously without pre-judging in either direction, and explores the family’s feelings, pressure and the child’s distress
Explains the proper process and why a prescription today is not appropriate, in a way that keeps the family engaged rather than dismissed

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges information-gathering and referral, addresses excluded contributors (e.g. hearing/sleep/safeguarding), supports the family, and reviews — properly-routed, non-pre-judging assessment

worked.lbl: Take it seriously, set the frame
worked.txt: "I can hear the school have been firm about this, and I take it seriously. But ADHD isn’t something I can diagnose or treat from a teacher’s report — it needs a proper specialist assessment. My job is to look at the whole picture and get Leo to the right people."
"Tell me what Leo’s like — is the restlessness and not-listening only at school, or at home too, with friends, all the time? When did it start? How’s it affecting his learning and friendships?"

"A few important checks, because several things can look like ADHD: how’s his hearing, his sleep, his reading and learning? Any worries or big changes at home? … These genuinely matter — we don’t want to miss something treatable."
"For a proper assessment we need information from school and home — some standard questionnaires filled in by you and his teachers. Let’s get those organised; they’re part of the referral."

"I’ll refer Leo to the specialist neurodevelopmental team. I’ll be honest — there’s usually a wait. If they diagnose ADHD, the first steps are information, support and changes at school and home; if he’s still struggling a lot once those are in place and reviewed, medication is a recognised option at his age, started by the specialists. Cutting out colourings or additives isn’t recommended as a treatment."

"Meanwhile, let’s get the school’s SENCO involved and I’ll point you to some support. How are YOU finding it? … Come back if things get harder, or if you notice anything about his hearing, sleep or mood, and we’ll keep things moving."

f.learning: When a school declares a child has ADHD and needs medication, the GP must neither dismiss the concern nor rubber-stamp it: ADHD is a clinical diagnosis made by a specialist neurodevelopmental service (paediatrics/CAMHS) after structured, multi-setting assessment, and is not diagnosed or medicated in primary care on a teacher’s report. Take the concern seriously and characterise the pattern — inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, their childhood onset, their pervasiveness across settings (present at home AND school, not only one), and the degree of impairment on learning, relationships and the child — since symptoms confined to one setting or explained by circumstances point away from ADHD. The key safety skill is to exclude and consider the many mimics and contributors: hearing or vision impairment (a child who cannot hear seems inattentive), sleep disorders (tired children are inattentive and hyperactive), learning difficulty, autism, anxiety or low mood, attachment difficulties, trauma and adverse childhood experiences, safeguarding concerns, and family or social stress — missing a hearing problem, a sleep disorder or a safeguarding issue while labelling "ADHD" is a serious error. Gather information from multiple sources (school reports and observations, standardised questionnaires completed by parents and teachers, developmental and family history) rather than acting on a single verbal report, and refer to the neurodevelopmental/ADHD pathway, managing expectations honestly: assessment takes time, diagnosis is specialist, and treatment is staged (NICE NG87): information, support and environmental modifications at school and home first, then — at age 5 and over — specialist-initiated medication if symptoms still cause persistent significant impairment after those modifications have been made and reviewed, not a GP-prescribed quick fix; elimination diets are not advised as a general treatment. Support the family meanwhile (school SENCO, behavioural strategies, support organisations; schools support on need without waiting for a diagnosis — SEND Code of Practice 2015). The hidden agenda is school pressure, parental exhaustion or feeling blamed, a wish for a label that brings help, possible family stress, the child’s distress, or fear of medication; take it seriously, do not pre-judge for or against ADHD, explore the wider picture, exclude mimics, support the family, and route it properly.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG87 (2018, updated 2019) · NICE QS39 · NICE CG128 · SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (DfE/DHSC 2015)
knowledge.summary: ADHD in a child is diagnosed by a specialist after a full assessment across settings. The GP does not diagnose it or start medication, but gathers the picture, screens for mimics and refers.

points.t: NICE NG87: primary care practitioners should not make the initial diagnosis or start medication in children with suspected ADHD. Diagnosis and medication start in secondary care (paediatrics, child psychiatry or a specialist ADHD/CAMHS service).

NICE NG87: if the problems are causing severe impairment, refer straight to secondary care. Where the impact is less than severe, a period of watchful waiting of up to 10 weeks can be considered before referral; follow the local neurodevelopmental pathway, which often needs school information with the referral.

NICE NG87: symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity and/or inattention that occur often, are present in 2 or more important settings (for a child, home and school), and cause at least moderate psychological, social and/or educational impairment. The diagnosis should not be made on rating scales or observation alone.

Hearing or vision problems, sleep difficulties (including snoring), specific learning difficulty, speech and language problems, autism (NICE CG128), anxiety or low mood, attachment difficulties, trauma or adverse experiences, and family stress. Safeguarding concerns must be asked about, not assumed away.

NICE NG87: give ADHD-focused information and support, and make environmental changes at school and home. At age 5 and over, medication is offered only if symptoms still cause persistent significant impairment in at least one domain after those modifications have been made and reviewed, and it is started by a specialist. Do not advise cutting out artificial colourings or additives as a general treatment.

points.h: School support does not wait for a label
points.t: SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (2015): schools should put support in place on the basis of need, through the SENCO, without waiting for a diagnosis. NICE QS39 sets out annual specialist review once medication is started.

dg.d: Open question to the mother; let her describe the school’s concerns and her request before responding.
Explored home life, family stress, the mother’s exhaustion and feeling blamed, and pressure from school.
Hearing test, vision check, sleep diary; parent and teacher questionnaires; school report for the referral.
ADHD vs single-setting behaviour, hearing or vision loss, sleep problems, learning or language difficulty, autism, anxiety, adverse experiences.
Screened sensitively for safeguarding and adverse experiences; asked about low mood, risk of exclusion and severe impairment.
Stated that ADHD is possible but not established; assessment across settings by a specialist is needed.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Referral to the neurodevelopmental pathway, no GP prescription, SENCO support now, parent support; medication specialist-led and not first.
Addressed the mother’s exhaustion; hearing and sleep followed up; learning needs flagged to school.
Review in about a month; clear route back if things worsen; referral chased if impairment increases.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’m worn out”, the mixed feelings about “strong tablets” and the lack of information about home behaviour.
Her idea (the school may be right), concern (blame, medication worries) and expectation (a prescription or “referral for tablets”).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — feeling blamed by school; worn out after a recent separation she doesn't want to discuss; torn about medication for her son — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Mrs Hartnell, it’s Dr Shah. Thanks for joining. Before I say anything, tell me in your own words what’s been happening with Leo and what the school have said.
model.why: Open question; lets her set out the story before any view is given

model.text: They say he’s got ADHD. He can’t sit still, he’s disruptive, he doesn’t listen. They reckon he needs medication and told me to come and get it sorted. Can you prescribe something, or refer him for the tablets?

It sounds as though the school have been pretty firm with you. I take what they’re seeing seriously, and I want to help you get to the bottom of it. Could I spend a few minutes understanding Leo as a whole, then explain how ADHD is assessed and agree what we do next?
model.why: Acknowledges the concern and sets a shared agenda without pre-judging

model.text: Okay. I just want something done.
Of course. Starting with school: what exactly do they see, and when did they first raise it?
model.why: Characterises the core features and onset

model.text: He can’t sit still, he’s disruptive, he doesn’t listen — that’s what they keep saying. I couldn’t tell you exactly when it started.
And what is he like at home, or with friends and at clubs? Is it the same everywhere, or mostly at school?
model.why: Tests pervasiveness across settings, which the diagnosis depends on

model.text: Honestly, I’m not sure. He’s a lively boy, but I’ve never really thought of it as a problem at home.
That’s helpful to know, and it’s exactly the sort of thing the specialists will ask about. How is it affecting him — his learning, his friendships, how he feels about himself?
model.why: Asks about impairment, not just symptoms

model.text: I don’t really know what he thinks. They haven’t said much about that side.
A few things can look very like ADHD, so I ask every family about them. Has his hearing or eyesight been checked recently? And how does he sleep — does he snore, or wake a lot?
model.why: Screens the common mimics: hearing, vision and sleep

model.text: Not that I know of, no one’s checked his hearing. Sleep, I’d have to think about.
How are his reading and writing compared with others in his class? And his talking and understanding when you explain things?
model.why: Screens for learning, speech and language difficulty

model.text: I’m not sure. I’d have to ask school.
I also ask everyone this, because worry and upheaval can show up as behaviour: has anything big changed for Leo, or for the family, and is everyone safe and okay at home?
model.why: Routine, non-accusatory screen for stress, trauma and safeguarding

model.text: Nothing I want to go into. It’s just me being worn out by it all.
You said you’re worn out. How are you doing with all of this?
model.why: Picks up the cue about her own exhaustion

model.text: I feel like they think it’s my fault. School are always on at me. I thought if I came back with tablets they’d get off my back.
That sounds exhausting, and I’m sorry you’ve felt blamed. Coming today shows you’re doing exactly what a caring parent does. What do you think is going on with Leo?
model.why: Validates her feelings and draws out her own idea

model.text: I don’t know. Part of me wonders if they’re right. Part of me doesn’t want him on strong tablets.

Both of those feelings make sense. Here’s how it works. ADHD is a real condition, but it can’t be diagnosed from a teacher’s report or by me in a GP appointment. A specialist team looks at how he is at home and at school, and rules out other things first. So I won’t prescribe today — not because I doubt you, but because medication must be started by that team.
model.why: Explains specialist diagnosis and why a GP prescription is not appropriate

model.text: So what happens, then? Do we just wait?

No, we get things moving now. I’ll refer Leo to the neurodevelopmental team. They’ll want questionnaires from you and from school — I’ll send those — and a report from his teacher. I’ll also arrange a hearing test, and I’d like you to keep a note of his sleep for a couple of weeks.
model.why: Multi-source information, referral and exclusion of hearing and sleep causes

model.text: How long does the referral take?

I’ll be honest — there’s usually a wait, often months. If they do diagnose ADHD, the first steps are support at school and at home, with advice for you as a parent. Medication is considered by the specialists if he is still struggling after that. It’s one option, not the starting point.
model.why: Manages expectations on timescales and staged treatment

model.text: While we wait, school don’t need a diagnosis to help him. Could you ask to meet the SENCO — the teacher who organises extra support — about his learning and any changes in class?
model.why: SEND support by need, without waiting for a label

model.text: I didn’t know I could ask for that.
You can. I’ll also give you details of support for parents. And I’d like to hear from Leo himself at some point — how school feels for him. Does that plan sound right to you?
model.why: Includes the child’s voice and checks the plan with her

model.text: Yes. It feels better than just being told to get tablets.

If things get much worse at school, if there’s a risk of exclusion, or if you notice him becoming very low, anxious or not sleeping, get back to me and I can chase the referral. And if you ever feel you’re not coping, please tell us — you matter here too.
model.why: Specific safety-net covering the child and the parent

model.text: Thank you, I will.
Can I check I’ve explained it clearly? What will you tell school when they phone next?
That the GP has referred him, that the specialists decide about ADHD and medicine, and that I want to meet the SENCO.
Perfect. I’ll book a review in about a month to see how the questionnaires and hearing test are going.

social.t: Repeated pressure from school, a parent who feels blamed and possible exhaustion. Ask about her support and wellbeing; parent support groups can help while waiting.

SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (2015): the SENCO can put in SEN support on the basis of need. An Education, Health and Care needs assessment can be requested if needs are greater; no diagnosis is required first.

legal.t: A child whose ADHD or other condition has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities may be disabled under the Act, and schools must make reasonable adjustments.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (HM Government, 2026) and NICE NG76 (child abuse and neglect): behaviour change can be a sign of maltreatment, so ask routinely and refer if concerned.

professional.t: NICE NG87: primary care does not diagnose ADHD or start medication in children. Continuing prescriptions happen only under a shared care arrangement after specialist initiation and titration.
GMC 0–18 years guidance: involve children in decisions about their care in a way that suits their age and understanding.

community.t: Local parent-carer forums, SENDIASS (free impartial SEND advice for families), and ADHD UK or ADDISS for information.
Disability Living Allowance for children can be claimed on the basis of care or supervision needs well beyond those of other children of the same age; a diagnosis is not required.

redFlags: Disclosure or signs of abuse, neglect or domestic abuse — follow safeguarding procedures the same day
Regression in skills, new neurological symptoms or episodes of staring or absence
Low mood, self-harm talk or severe anxiety in the child
Risk of permanent exclusion or a parent who is not coping
psychosocial: Home and school: is the behaviour in both settings or only one?
Impact on learning, friendships and self-esteem
Family changes, stress and the parent’s own wellbeing
ice: Idea: “School say it’s ADHD — maybe they’re right”
Concern: being blamed; not wanting her son on “strong tablets”
Expectation: a prescription or a referral “for the tablets”

playbook.diagnosis: “ADHD is possible, and it’s also possible something else is behind this, such as hearing, sleep or learning difficulties. It’s diagnosed by a specialist team who look at how Leo is at home and at school.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a jigsaw. School have given us one important piece. The specialists need the pieces from home, from his hearing and sleep, and from his learning before they can see the whole picture.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel blamed and worn out. This isn’t your fault, and getting a proper assessment is the best thing you can do for Leo.”
management.psychosocial: Get school support started now through the SENCO, offer parent support, and check in on her own coping.
sharedPlan: Referral to the neurodevelopmental pathway with parent and teacher questionnaires and a school report
Hearing test, vision check and a sleep diary
No GP prescribing; explain staged treatment with medication specialist-led
safetyNet: Return sooner if behaviour worsens, exclusion looms, or Leo seems low, anxious or not sleeping
Review in about a month; chase the referral if impairment increases

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can stand between a school’s certainty and a worried parent without taking either side too early. Candidates fail by prescribing, by dismissing, or by forgetting the mimics.

items.fail: Agreeing to “refer for the tablets” or suggesting a trial of medication.
items.why: NICE NG87: primary care does not diagnose ADHD or start medication in children. A plan built on a teacher’s view alone is unsafe.
items.fix: “I can’t prescribe for ADHD, and I wouldn’t want to until a specialist has assessed him properly. Here’s how we get that started today.”

items.fail: Never asking about home, so the pattern is known in only one setting.
items.why: The diagnosis needs symptoms in 2 or more settings with impairment. Without this, the referral has little value.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Is he like this at home, with friends, at clubs?” and collect questionnaires from both parent and teacher.

items.fail: No screen for hearing, sleep, learning difficulty or family stress.
items.why: Missing a treatable mimic while the family waits months for assessment is a serious error and a common examiner comment.
items.fix: Arrange a hearing test and sleep diary, and ask about reading, language and big changes at home.

items.fail: Asking “Is something going on at home?” in a tone that implies blame.
items.why: She already feels blamed. A clumsy safeguarding question loses her trust and the chance of a real answer.
items.fix: Normalise it: “I ask every family this…” then ask about changes and whether everyone is safe.

items.fail: Talking only about Leo and never about his mother’s exhaustion.
items.why: Her hidden agenda is pressure and feeling blamed. Missing it is a Relating to Others miss.
items.fix: “How are you doing with all of this?” Then reflect it back in the plan.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll refer and see” and no interim support or safety-net.
items.why: Waits are long. A plan with nothing for the meantime is incomplete.
items.fix: SENCO support now, parent support, named reasons to return, and a review date.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes or promises medication, or dismisses the school (“all boys are lively”); no question about home behaviour, hearing, sleep or safety; no referral or a referral with no information; mother leaves feeling blamed.
wordPics.pass: Explains that ADHD is diagnosed by a specialist after assessment across settings; asks about home and school; screens some mimics; refers to the neurodevelopmental pathway; mentions school support and gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks about hearing, vision, sleep, learning, stress and safety in a routine, non-accusatory way; names the mother’s exhaustion and sense of blame; organises questionnaires and a hearing test; explains staged treatment honestly; gets the SENCO involved now; seeks Leo’s own view; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.instead: "The school’s view matters, and it’s one part of the picture. A specialist team looks at home and school together before anyone decides."

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t know. Part of me wonders if they’re right. Part of me doesn’t want him on strong tablets.

Both of those feelings make sense. Here’s how it works. ADHD is a real condition, but it can’t be diagnosed from a teacher’s report or by me in a GP appointment. A specialist team looks at how he is at home and at school, and rules out other things first. So I won’t prescribe today — not because I doubt you, but because medication must be started by that team.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains specialist diagnosis and why a GP prescription is not appropriate

SCA_MODELS.text: So what happens, then? Do we just wait?

No, we get things moving now. I’ll refer Leo to the neurodevelopmental team. They’ll want questionnaires from you and from school — I’ll send those — and a report from his teacher. I’ll also arrange a hearing test, and I’d like you to keep a note of his sleep for a couple of weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Multi-source information, referral and exclusion of hearing and sleep causes

SCA_MODELS.text: How long does the referral take?

I’ll be honest — there’s usually a wait, often months. If they do diagnose ADHD, the first steps are support at school and at home, with advice for you as a parent. Medication is considered by the specialists if he is still struggling after that. It’s one option, not the starting point.
SCA_MODELS.why: Manages expectations on timescales and staged treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: While we wait, school don’t need a diagnosis to help him. Could you ask to meet the SENCO — the teacher who organises extra support — about his learning and any changes in class?
SCA_MODELS.why: SEND support by need, without waiting for a label

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know I could ask for that.
You can. I’ll also give you details of support for parents. And I’d like to hear from Leo himself at some point — how school feels for him. Does that plan sound right to you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Includes the child’s voice and checks the plan with her

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. It feels better than just being told to get tablets.

If things get much worse at school, if there’s a risk of exclusion, or if you notice him becoming very low, anxious or not sleeping, get back to me and I can chase the referral. And if you ever feel you’re not coping, please tell us — you matter here too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net covering the child and the parent

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, I will.
Can I check I’ve explained it clearly? What will you tell school when they phone next?
That the GP has referred him, that the specialists decide about ADHD and medicine, and that I want to meet the SENCO.
Perfect. I’ll book a review in about a month to see how the questionnaires and hearing test are going.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG87 (2018, updated 2019) · NICE QS39 · NICE CG128 · SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (DfE/DHSC 2015)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: ADHD in a child is diagnosed by a specialist after a full assessment across settings. The GP does not diagnose it or start medication, but gathers the picture, screens for mimics and refers.

points.t: NICE NG87: primary care practitioners should not make the initial diagnosis or start medication in children with suspected ADHD. Diagnosis and medication start in secondary care (paediatrics, child psychiatry or a specialist ADHD/CAMHS service).

NICE NG87: if the problems are causing severe impairment, refer straight to secondary care. Where the impact is less than severe, a period of watchful waiting of up to 10 weeks can be considered before referral; follow the local neurodevelopmental pathway, which often needs school information with the referral.

NICE NG87: symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity and/or inattention that occur often, are present in 2 or more important settings (for a child, home and school), and cause at least moderate psychological, social and/or educational impairment. The diagnosis should not be made on rating scales or observation alone.

Hearing or vision problems, sleep difficulties (including snoring), specific learning difficulty, speech and language problems, autism (NICE CG128), anxiety or low mood, attachment difficulties, trauma or adverse experiences, and family stress. Safeguarding concerns must be asked about, not assumed away.

NICE NG87: give ADHD-focused information and support, and make environmental changes at school and home. At age 5 and over, medication is offered only if symptoms still cause persistent significant impairment in at least one domain after those modifications have been made and reviewed, and it is started by a specialist. Do not advise cutting out artificial colourings or additives as a general treatment.

points.h: School support does not wait for a label
points.t: SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (2015): schools should put support in place on the basis of need, through the SENCO, without waiting for a diagnosis. NICE QS39 sets out annual specialist review once medication is started.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to the mother; let her describe the school’s concerns and her request before responding.
Explored home life, family stress, the mother’s exhaustion and feeling blamed, and pressure from school.
Picked up “I’m worn out”, the mixed feelings about “strong tablets” and the lack of information about home behaviour.
Her idea (the school may be right), concern (blame, medication worries) and expectation (a prescription or “referral for tablets”).
Hearing test, vision check, sleep diary; parent and teacher questionnaires; school report for the referral.
ADHD vs single-setting behaviour, hearing or vision loss, sleep problems, learning or language difficulty, autism, anxiety, adverse experiences.
Screened sensitively for safeguarding and adverse experiences; asked about low mood, risk of exclusion and severe impairment.
Stated that ADHD is possible but not established; assessment across settings by a specialist is needed.
Referral to the neurodevelopmental pathway, no GP prescription, SENCO support now, parent support; medication specialist-led and not first.
Addressed the mother’s exhaustion; hearing and sleep followed up; learning needs flagged to school.
Review in about a month; clear route back if things worsen; referral chased if impairment increases.

social.t: Repeated pressure from school, a parent who feels blamed and possible exhaustion. Ask about her support and wellbeing; parent support groups can help while waiting.

SEND Code of Practice 0 to 25 (2015): the SENCO can put in SEN support on the basis of need. An Education, Health and Care needs assessment can be requested if needs are greater; no diagnosis is required first.

legal.t: A child whose ADHD or other condition has a substantial and long-term effect on day-to-day activities may be disabled under the Act, and schools must make reasonable adjustments.
Working Together to Safeguard Children (HM Government, 2026) and NICE NG76 (child abuse and neglect): behaviour change can be a sign of maltreatment, so ask routinely and refer if concerned.

professional.t: NICE NG87: primary care does not diagnose ADHD or start medication in children. Continuing prescriptions happen only under a shared care arrangement after specialist initiation and titration.
GMC 0–18 years guidance: involve children in decisions about their care in a way that suits their age and understanding.

community.t: Local parent-carer forums, SENDIASS (free impartial SEND advice for families), and ADHD UK or ADDISS for information.
Disability Living Allowance for children can be claimed on the basis of care or supervision needs well beyond those of other children of the same age; a diagnosis is not required.

redFlags: Disclosure or signs of abuse, neglect or domestic abuse — follow safeguarding procedures the same day
Regression in skills, new neurological symptoms or episodes of staring or absence
Low mood, self-harm talk or severe anxiety in the child
Risk of permanent exclusion or a parent who is not coping
psychosocial: Home and school: is the behaviour in both settings or only one?
Impact on learning, friendships and self-esteem
Family changes, stress and the parent’s own wellbeing
ice: Idea: “School say it’s ADHD — maybe they’re right”
Concern: being blamed; not wanting her son on “strong tablets”
Expectation: a prescription or a referral “for the tablets”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “ADHD is possible, and it’s also possible something else is behind this, such as hearing, sleep or learning difficulties. It’s diagnosed by a specialist team who look at how Leo is at home and at school.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a jigsaw. School have given us one important piece. The specialists need the pieces from home, from his hearing and sleep, and from his learning before they can see the whole picture.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel blamed and worn out. This isn’t your fault, and getting a proper assessment is the best thing you can do for Leo.”
management.psychosocial: Get school support started now through the SENCO, offer parent support, and check in on her own coping.
sharedPlan: Referral to the neurodevelopmental pathway with parent and teacher questionnaires and a school report
Hearing test, vision check and a sleep diary
No GP prescribing; explain staged treatment with medication specialist-led
safetyNet: Return sooner if behaviour worsens, exclusion looms, or Leo seems low, anxious or not sleeping
Review in about a month; chase the referral if impairment increases

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can stand between a school’s certainty and a worried parent without taking either side too early. Candidates fail by prescribing, by dismissing, or by forgetting the mimics.

items.fail: Agreeing to “refer for the tablets” or suggesting a trial of medication.
items.why: NICE NG87: primary care does not diagnose ADHD or start medication in children. A plan built on a teacher’s view alone is unsafe.
items.fix: “I can’t prescribe for ADHD, and I wouldn’t want to until a specialist has assessed him properly. Here’s how we get that started today.”

items.fail: Never asking about home, so the pattern is known in only one setting.
items.why: The diagnosis needs symptoms in 2 or more settings with impairment. Without this, the referral has little value.
items.fix: Ask directly: “Is he like this at home, with friends, at clubs?” and collect questionnaires from both parent and teacher.

items.fail: No screen for hearing, sleep, learning difficulty or family stress.
items.why: Missing a treatable mimic while the family waits months for assessment is a serious error and a common examiner comment.
items.fix: Arrange a hearing test and sleep diary, and ask about reading, language and big changes at home.

items.fail: Asking “Is something going on at home?” in a tone that implies blame.
items.why: She already feels blamed. A clumsy safeguarding question loses her trust and the chance of a real answer.
items.fix: Normalise it: “I ask every family this…” then ask about changes and whether everyone is safe.

items.fail: Talking only about Leo and never about his mother’s exhaustion.
items.why: Her hidden agenda is pressure and feeling blamed. Missing it is a Relating to Others miss.
items.fix: “How are you doing with all of this?” Then reflect it back in the plan.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll refer and see” and no interim support or safety-net.
items.why: Waits are long. A plan with nothing for the meantime is incomplete.
items.fix: SENCO support now, parent support, named reasons to return, and a review date.
